group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man was evaluated in the pre-operative medicine suite this afternoon in anticipation of an open right hemi-hepatectomy scheduled in three days for a 9 cm segment VII hepatocellular carcinoma that has remained confined to the liver on staging CT and PET imaging; the surgical and anesthesia teams expect a long upper abdominal incision, prolonged parenchymal transection with intermittent low central venous pressure technique, and the possibility of substantial blood loss, all of which raise concern for peri-operative hemodynamic stress. The patient arrived by wheelchair from radiology but walked unassisted into the examination room, stating that over the past month he has felt “sluggish” with exertion and needs to pause after climbing a single flight of stairs because of fatigue and mild breathlessness, symptoms he attributes to his “weak heart.” Review of cardiovascular history revealed that six years ago he was diagnosed with a dilated left ventricle after an episode of influenza-associated myocarditis; echocardiography performed three months ago documented an end-diastolic diameter of 6.8 cm and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32 %, with global hypokinesis and no segmental wall motion abnormality. He has required two hospital admissions in the past year for intravenous diuretics when lower-extremity edema and exertional dyspnea progressed despite home therapy; between admissions he follows a low-sodium diet and weighs himself daily, reporting that he has remained within 2 kg of his baseline over the last four weeks. Medications taken this morning include carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg each morning, torsemide 20 mg every other day, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg. He denies ever experiencing substernal chest pressure, radiation of discomfort to the arm or jaw, diaphoresis at rest, or prior positive stress imaging; a nuclear perfusion scan performed eighteen months earlier showed no reversible ischemia. He has never undergone percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary bypass and has not been told that he has coronary calcifications on prior imaging studies. There is no personal history of transient neurologic symptoms, carotid surgery, or cerebrovascular accident. Additional chronic conditions include stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to longstanding hypertension, non-proliferative retinopathy without visual impairment, and compensated alcoholic cirrhosis (Child–Pugh A) after abstaining from alcohol for the past four years; he smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for twenty years but quit a decade ago and now uses no tobacco or recreational drugs. Family history is notable for a father with congestive cardiomyopathy of unknown etiology in his seventies and a mother with rheumatoid arthritis; there are no known premature cardiac deaths. Vital signs today: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 86 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 % breathing ambient air, and oral temperature 36.9 °C. His body mass index is 26 kg/m². On inspection he appears euvolemic with no accessory muscle use. Jugular venous pulsation is seen 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees. The apical impulse is displaced laterally in the sixth intercostal space, and auscultation reveals a soft S3 gallop without murmurs. Bibasilar crackles are absent, lungs are clear throughout, and there is trace pitting edema at both ankles. Abdominal examination displays a firm, non-tender liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin but no ascites. Neurologic examination is non-focal with intact cranial nerves and normal strength. Laboratory studies acquired two hours before the visit demonstrate hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.8 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 165 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL, consistent with values documented over the preceding six months; estimated glomerular filtration rate by CKD-EPI is 46 mL/min/1.73 m². Aspartate aminotransferase is 48 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 42 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 180 U/L, total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Fasting glucose this morning was 132 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c checked last month was 6.9 %. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows sinus rhythm at 84 beats per minute with left bundle branch block and no acute ST-segment deviations. Upright posterior–anterior chest radiograph demonstrates a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, clear lung fields, and flattened costophrenic angles, without pulmonary vascular congestion. The most recent transthoracic echocardiogram additionally noted mild functional mitral regurgitation and a right ventricular systolic pressure of 38 mm Hg. Airway assessment points to a Mallampati class II view, satisfactory mouth opening, and good neck extension. After discussion of peri-operative strategies—including continuation of beta-blockade, cautious preload management, intra-operative transesophageal echo availability, and consideration for postoperative telemetry in a monitored bed—the patient verbalized understanding and remains motivated to proceed with surgery.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns one point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: open hemi-hepatectomy is intraperitoneal surgery → 1.
- History of heart failure: dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 32% and prior admissions for congestion → 1, even though he is currently compensated.
- Ischemic heart disease: none documented; the cardiomyopathy followed myocarditis → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: none; elevated glucose alone does not count → 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL → 0.
Sum: 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
